title: Why Romantasy Suits a Sapphic Story So Well
body:
The genre's engines — power under constraint, courts that punish desire, magic that responds to feeling — map naturally onto two women falling in love in a world built to prevent it. The stakes need no invention; the world supplies them.

What I try to add is joy. The Sending Boat is about escape, but it is also about the specific happiness of being seen by the right person at the wrong time.

title: Sunken Kingdoms and the Weight of the Past
body:
The Drowned Kingdom takes its title literally: a court beneath the sea, holding onto crowns nobody living has seen. Fantasy lets a writer make the past a physical place, and romance lets her ask what it costs to leave it.

Betrayal in the book is not a twist; it is the pressure that the past exerts on anyone trying to choose a future.

title: Lost Selves, Chosen Families
body:
The Last Wondrous Isle closes the loop: an island where people go to forget, and a woman who arrives to remember. The chosen-family theme in queer fiction is often written as consolation; I wanted to write it as an adventure.

The family you choose is the crew you sail with — and the ship has to be worth boarding.
